speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, there is no reference as to whose drawing board it is on. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED DEVELOPMENT OF NEW REGIONAL BOMB
speechtext: The hon. member has not really brought out any fact which indicates responsibility on the part of any member of the ministry sitting in this house, but if he wishes to ask a specific minister whether he has such an instrument on his drawing board I think the question would be permitted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED DEVELOPMENT OF NEW REGIONAL BOMB

subtopic: REPORTED DEVELOPMENT OF NEW REGIONAL BOMB

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF TALKS CONCERNING TESTS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF TALKS CONCERNING TESTS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and ask if he is in a position to give the house any information regarding the resumption of nuclear test talks. I ask this question because of the minister's well known interest in the restriction of nuclear weapons in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF TALKS CONCERNING TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the house is fully aware, this government remains firmly opposed to the testing of nuclear and thermonuclear weapons. Agreement among the nuclear powers on a definitive cessation of such tests under effective international control would give a welcome assurance that the world would be safeguarded against the hazards they entail. Therefore we are greatly encouraged by the many indications there are that the United States will put forward new and far reaching proposals in a sincere attempt to bridge the remaining differences that separate them from the U.S.S.R. in this field.
This development brings fresh hope to governments and peoples in all countries, large and small, whose interests are so intimately caught up in the success or failure of the Geneva talks. I understand that it will take some days for the new United States position to be outlined in its entirety to the Soviet side. Of course during that period we will be watching with interest and concern to see how the U.S.S.R. will respond to these advances.
As the hon. member for Essex East knows, these talks were commenced in October, 1958, I think it was, and during that time there has been a moratorium on further nuclear tests by the three nations engaged in the talks. This moratorium continues today. We are very hopeful that there will be beneficial results when the talks are resumed.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF TALKS CONCERNING TESTS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. In view of the hon. gentleman's well known position, as well as that of the government, that there should be a cessation of nuclear tests, may I ask the hon. gentleman if it is the policy of the government to continue to oppose any extension of the countries that might become possessors of nuclear weapons?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF TALKS CONCERNING TESTS
speechtext:
Well, now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman, as he quite often does, laid a foundation and then asked a question that was not related to that foundation at all but

to an entirely different subject. This government, as I say, has been against any further nuclear tests and that continues to be the policy.

Inquiries of the Ministry knowledge that under the Trans-Canada Highway Act, which was enacted in 1949, contributions by the federal government to any part of a highway used in any province and built before 1949 are allowed; but with respect to any part of a highway subsequently used by a province as part of the trans-Canada highway which was built after the act came into force but before that province came into the scheme as a member under contract to build the trans-Canada highway, that part of the highway, of course, cannot qualify for payments from the dominion government. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night at ten o'clock I had given the reasons which, in my opinion, have caused a slow-down in our economy and provoked unemployment. I should like for a moment to comment on this very question of unemployment and to give my opinion on the seriousness of this problem.
There is no doubt that the present number of unemployed is far too great; in fact any unemployment at all is undesirable in a wealthy country such as Canada. It is obvious, however, that the present figures do not indicate the real nature of the problem, and are so made up as to exaggerate its importance. In a well documented speech made in this house on March 9 last the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) gave us a breakdown of the unemployment figure which is worthy of note. The statistical figures to which he referred indicate that about 20 per cent of the jobless are young people still in their teens. It is obvious that the labour market is unusually crowded by thousands of young people who normally should be in school in order to prepare themselves for the tasks of life. These statistics also show that the proportion of unemployed is much higher among non-specialized workers than among those who have trades. This is why many advantages will result from the technical and vocational training program which is now in force.
It is obvious also, in view of the fact that the number of farm workers has been reduced by 300,000 over the last 10 years, that automation on the farm has taken its toll of farm workers, who now must look to the cities in order to find work. It is therefore urgent to educate those young people and give them trades in order to give them the chance they deserve to find a place for themselves in the nation's industries.
It also seems that the labour market is employing a greater number of women and the rate of unemployment among women is

less than the rate among men. While the female population has provided almost half the labour force in the last few years, it has suffered much less than the male population from economic fluctuations. The number of married women drawing unemployment insurance under present conditions is abnormally high, and the increase of female labour in the labour market presents a sociological problem which those who analyse the employment situation should study very closely.

One thing is certain, Mr. Speaker-there is too much unemployment.

-the situation is the result of events shaped by the second world war and the period which followed the victory in 1945.
Mr. Speaker, at this point in my remarks, let me say to the leader of the government, his ministers and supporters in this house, that they started off by denying this matter of unemployment.
Last September, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) finally admitted in one of his great T.V. performances that he was beginning to worry about unemployment. Later, some said there were some big bad wolves who were responsible for the unemployment situation. Yesterday, the Associate Minister of National Defence indicated that the situation was the result of events during world war II.
When I examine those statements, I cannot help but say that all the members of the cabinet have a logic that kills.
If we analyse the period after world war II we find that there were only two years at the most where the percentage of unemployed was in excess of 3 per cent, and I mean 1954 and 1955.
Recalling the letter sent about a year or a year and a half ago to the Montreal Gazette by Mr. Forsyth of the Canadian Labour Congress and admitting that he is an expert in the matter, we can say that a country enjoys full employment when unemployment does not exceed 3 per cent.

The remarks I intend to make this afternoon do not particularly concern the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) whom I hold in great esteem. I think he is quite a sensible man.
My remarks are directed to his colleagues in the cabinet-the cabinet as a whole. I know that the Minister of Labour has a better grasp of the unemployment problem. If he did not put to use all the ideas he had for solving this problem, it was not his fault.
I can admit with my colleagues that the government did make certain attempts to cope with this situation which we consider regrettably contrary to what certain ministers and members have said.
I do not mind-as a certain well-spoken member would say-sitting on this side of the house. Our common duty is to serve our country well.
It is with that in mind that we rise to discuss problems which affect or should affect us all.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the Minister of Labour have brought forward a resolution, a program that would extend accelerated depreciation to industries being set up in certain areas. I shall not call them distressed areas; this is something else and I shall say a few words about it, because the Associate Minister of National Defence accused us of referring to distressed areas, when those terms are the very ones used in the resolution submitted to us. I have been in Ottawa nearly eight years and I have never heard anyone here speak about distressed areas. This is the first time I have seen this expression in any legislation introduced by the government and it is the government that is suggesting it. The Financial Post, to which my leader referred yesterday, has expressed its views on the government measure now submitted. As a matter of fact, in an article published on March 18, Mr. J. G. MacDonald stated this:
(Text):
We find it difficult to believe that the government could seriously consider the new regulation as a genuine tax incentive.
Because the prospect to inducing the commencement of a new manufacturing enterprise in a depressed area would be bleak even to those companies already established, it is unlikely that any outsider will be induced by the new regulation to risk his capital when local businessmen are not prepared to do so.
The regulation would probably make sense if it enabled established manufacturers in depressed areas to qualify for additional capital cost allowances in respect of new product development of their own.
The department directive, however, makes it clear that capital equipment acquired to produce new products resulting from change, redesign or innovation will not be qualified under the new regulation.

Change, redesign and innovation are, of course, the principal methods by which existing manufacturers in depressed areas improve their products and increase their production and sales.
(Translation):
As I was saying a moment ago, we admit that the government made some efforts but this is not enough in view of the seriousness of the problem that has been with us for some months.
This reminds me of an appalling thought expressed by John Stuart Mills:
When the welfare of a whole country is at stake, half-measures do not produce partial results; they produce no results whatsoever.
Even though the government has made certain attempts to solve the unemployment problem, not only is the situation not improving, it is getting worse.
We are told from time to time that unemployment is only seasonal; let us wait for spring, let us wait for the crows. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the greatest abettors of socialism and communism in our country, and in other western countries, are those men who are in power but who only sit back on government benches waiting until the return of the crows or of spring to remedy a situation such as this.
We are asked to make proposals from time to time. Well, I have two suggestions to submit to the government. I am sure they will be welcome because they are not my own. The first was made by the Prime Minister himself. We all remember the year 1957 because that year we, from the Liberal party, were shifted to this side so we could think things over. However, we have made good use of the period elapsed since June 10. The Prime Minister then went all over the country telling us that not enough of our raw materials were being processed in Canada. I might quote for instance what he said in Parry Sound-Muskoka on May 10, 1957:
(Text):
A Conservative government would do its best to assure that a larger share of irreplaceable raw materials was processed in Canada "for the benefit of Canadians and to ensure employment".
(Translation):
It was the same thing throughout Canada. And finally, in Saskatoon, he made the following statement, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of May 28:
(Text):
Raw materials taken to the United States for processing-with large quantities of the ultimate products being returned for sale in Canada- supplied employment to thousands of Americans, jobs which through a policy to encourage more processing in Canada would be held by Canadians.

(Translation):
I agree with the Prime Minister. I am sure that if the government supports the establishment of industries so that more of our raw materials are processed at home, not only will it reduce our trade imbalance with our neighbours to the south, as he himself stated during the election campaign of 1957, but it will also provide jobs for thousands of Canadians.
I should like to make another suggestion concerning my own area. But first I wish to pay tribute to my colleague from Chicoutimi (Mr. Brassard), and also to the mayor of Chicoutimi who have both made similar statements on the deepening of the Saguenay river. The Saguenay, my own area, is now hard hit by unemployment. We are having a hard time trying to convince new industries to settle in our area because we are quite a ways from large centres. Then too, there is the matter of freight rates. Recently, we met with the president of a company who immediately brought up the matter.
If the government would accept the suggestion made by one of its own members, seconded by the humble member for the neighbouring riding, to deepen the Saguenay river, we would not be put in a more favourable situation than elsewhere, but we would simply be raised to the level of all the other areas in the country. We would then have a chance attract industries, which would help us to fight the distressing situation in which we find ourselves today. It will be said that the deepening of the Saguenay river will be very costly. We will be told: "You Liberals are against deficit budgeting; each time a deficit budget is brought down, you criticize us." Let me say that neither my leader, nor my colleagues, nor anybody else is opposed to a deficit when such a deficit helps give new impetus to the national economy. We are not against deficits when they are designed to alleviate unemployment or to strengthen our national economy.
In the speech he delivered yesterday, our leader put forward proposals which are sensible and practical. He mentioned the establishment of a bank which would provide the municipalities with better credit facilities. I think his program was quite to the point. Laugh if you will and say: "You could have done that when you were here." To my mind, the situation is not the same, far from it. The worst reproach that can be addressed to the present government-and I am not referring to the Minister of Labour-is that it is neither right nor left of centre, nor even in the centre, but nowhere at all. Much has been said, Mr. Speaker, against socialism and communism. Long speeches are made about it. I heard one recently, at the Chateau Frontenac, about free enterprise. Let us fight shy of sluggishness, apathy and carelessness; they are leading straight and fast to dangers we are all trying to ward off, outright socialism and communism. It is useless and childish to make long speeches in praise of liberty, moral and spiritual values and private enterprise, in front of three quarters of a million people who are unable to earn their living. Our system will prove its superiority over other systems, thanks to its ability of getting effectively rid of the social evils which threaten it. I am not referring only to Canada but to many western nations. Unless the situation improves-and it will not unless the government resorts to measures quite more drastic and bold than the ones it has already introduced-there is the danger, as a writer has said, that the people who suffer will soon consider it is better to be a slave and not to work than to be free and have to work.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the government and those responsible for the administration of the country, to take a closer look at our problems. I know that they understand them, but if they understand them well, they must find bolder solutions than those already offered; I mean solutions that would actually improve the situation that has prevailed in recent months.

Mr. Speaker, I was also saying that yesterday the Leader of the Opposition dealt at length with the unemployment situation. He referred to the years 1955 and 1956, and again to the years 1960 and 1961.
In 1955 and 1956, we had an unemployment problem, yet our friends opposite were then in office. In 1955, 1956 and 1957, the Liberal administration had a chance to do something to remedy the situation, but they did nothing.

Mr. Speaker, to confirm that there was an unemployment situation in 1955 and 1956, I only have to refer to statistics published in the Canada Labour Gazette. As a matter of fact, as reported in volume LVII of that publication, for 1957, there were 89,800 unemployed in the Atlantic area as at February 14. This was an increase of 14.8 per cent over the previous month, and 16.3 per cent over the previous year. During the same period, in the Quebec area, there were 176,900 unemployed, an increase of 10.4 per cent over the previous month and of 13.7 per cent over the previous year. The prairies with 78,100 unemployed, had an increase of 6.3 per cent over the previous month and a decrease of 0.6 per cent from the previous year; the Pacific region, with an unemployed population of 71,400, had an increase of 39.2 per cent over the previous month and 7.5 per cent over the previous year. On February 14, 1957, the total unemployed population numbered 574,700 an increase of 9.2 per cent over the previous month and 11.5 per cent over the previous year. Furthermore, on February 1, 1957, the number of claimants for unemployment benefits was 545,981, or an increase of 37.1 per cent over the previous month and 14.5 per cent over the previous year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, those figures indicate that an unemployment crisis prevailed in the years 1955, 1956 and 1957, and that the government of the day not only failed to act as it ought to have done to remedy the situation, but that it merely misled the people, by not pointing out prevailing conditions and more particularly by failing to reveal to the Canadian people the economic report prepared at the time.
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition admitted yesterday that things were picking up. Speaking of the economic recession, he said that it had a tendancy to ebb away, and I entirely agree with him. As a matter of fact, he mentioned it before when speaking in London, Ontario. This is what I read in the newspaper Dimanche Matin, March 12, 1961:
If Mr. Pearson says that things are picking up, the recession must be at an end.
Mr. Pearson, leader of the Liberal party stated during the week end, in London Ont., that the number one problem which Canada has to face at this time, is that of economic recovery. However, there are some indications that the recession is about to end.
Always in connection with this matter, this is what Le Soleil of Saturday, March 11, 1961, had to say:
Canadian business recovery is expected in mid-1961.

"The slump which started about the middle of 1960, will probably keep on during the first months of 1961, but some improvement can be expected towards the middle of the year," stated Mr. E. S. Morse, president of the Investment Dealers' Association of Canada on a visit here.
It is expected that capital demand will be as strong in 1961 as in 1960. Federal government borrowing more particularly, will reach a much higher level. Mr. Morse expressed the view that there would be no new increase in interest rates for long term loans, but rather a trend to lower rates during the year.
Mentioning the trade situation, Mr. Morse stated that our export trade was rather encouraging, though some countries affected by the war have now completed their reconstruction and become major competitors on the world market. "In the future we will have a large measure of success in this field as long as we apply the latest methods and use the latest equipment, while controlling costs. Obviously, we will be helped by the reduction of the Canadian dollar premium," he added.
The Canadian dollar premium, which has been in existence for such a long time mainly resulted from provincial and municipal borrowing abroad, and of foreign capital investments in Canada made attractive by our high interest rates and development advantages. In the baby budget of last December, the federal government removed some tax exemptions formerly granted in order to attract foreign capital investment to this country. That decision had an immediate impact on the demand for Canadian dollars resulting in a sharp decrease of the premium. In time, our industry as well as our export trade will benefit from it.
Those are flattering words for the policy of this government.
Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that the recession had started under the administration of our hon. friends opposite. To prove it, I will quote from Le Devoir of Saturday, October 22, 1960:
The economic depression started in 1949.
"The resolution to unemployment is quite simple: save!"-Mr. Coyne.
Mr. James Coyne, governor of the Bank of Canada, has just published his annual report for 1960. It is an explosive document that will be discussed for a long time. In fact. Mr. Coyne has smashed the myth of the rosy years of the last decade. Mr. C. D. Howe must have turned in his grave on hearing the iconoclast raze to the ground the monument of infallibility erected to him by propaganda.
Mr. Speaker, we can see that the recession did not start with the coming into office of this government. And the Leader of the Opposition said that this government has done nothing, has adopted no measure to meet the situation.
As for the hon. member who spoke just before me, he pointed out that this government has done something but not enough.
Yet no government has ever done more to meet the situation than the present one. May I mention a few of those measures, so that this house and all the people in Canada may fully realize what this government has done to cope with the present situation.

Let us start with the housing situation. A down payment of $500 on a $10,000 house, as compared to $1,000 before. A down payment of $550 on an $11,000 house, as compared to $1,100 before. A down payment of $600 on a $12,000 house, compared to $1,200 before. The maximum loan has been raised from $12,800 to $14,200 and $14,900. One and a half million dollars have been provided for new housing. The federal government will pay 75 per cent of the costs of urban redevelopment and slum clearance. The government is providing $50 million for this purpose. House improvement loans are guaranteed up to $500 million, as compared to $200 million last year. Loans authorized for rental housing are increased from 80 to 85 per cent of value.
A second measure, against pollution: loans to municipalities for sewage plants; the government is making $100 million available for this.
In, the automobile industry: a reduction of the preferential tariff on imported automobiles and parts.
For small businesses. Loans up to $25,000 to enterprises with a gross annual income of $250,000. An amount of $300 million is provided for a three-year period to help small businesses in Canada, and especially the tourist industry.
As regards winter works in municipalities, the federal government will pay an amount of $30 million in the course of this winter. Works totalling over $200 million were approved in early December. In early December, employment was assured for more than 75,000 workers.
With regard to the training of the unemployed, the federal government will pay 75 per cent, that is to say it has paid 75 per cent of the cost of such training.
On vocational and technical training, there is a 50 per cent increase in training facilities in Canada. The federal government is paying 75 per cent of the cost of new schools up to 1963, and 50 per cent thereafter. Twenty six million dollars have been voted for vocational training this year, an increase of $9 million. Fifteen million dollars will be spent on new school construction.
On public works, there is a $100 million construction program.
On export credits, there is an immediate credit of up to $110 million to help finance Canadian exports abroad; an ultimate credit of $750 million.

The national productivity council aims at increasing productivity in Canada through labour-management co-operation, so that the country may keep up with competition.
On small businesses: There is a reduction in the corporation tax, in the case of small businesses, by raising from $25,000 to $35,000 the minimum above which the excess profit rate applies. The tax will be 21 per cent up to $35,000, whereas the rate on excess profits used to be 50 per cent on $25,000 and over.
On new industries, double depreciation is applicable in the case of goods not previously made in Canada. Double depreciation is applicable in the case of businesses locating in areas of greatest unemployment.
On foreign investments, there is a 15 per cent tax on profits of Canadian subsidiaries of non-resident corporations. By 1963, investment firms will have to get 75 per cent of their income from dividends of Canadian firms.
On investments in Canada: There is the removal of the 4 per cent extra tax as a means of stimulating investment in Canada.
On education, university students are allowed to deduct tuition fees from their taxable income.
On veterans' pensions, there is a 20 per cent increase.
There is also a return to parity of the Canadian dollar.

This particular program of double depreciation for depressed areas in principle, when it was first enunciated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), did give many people reason to believe that at long last the government had embarked on a substantially positive program to deal with unemployment, particularly in chronically unemployed areas, 90205-6-202J

as the Minister of Finance calls them or distressed areas as I call them. In principle, this program of double depreciation is sound. It was recommended by the Leader of the Opposition, speaking on behalf of this party, many months ago and it was reaffirmed at our national rally. It has been practised in the United Kingdom and in the United States, and in that latter country it has now become much stronger and more substantive in form. The Leader of the Opposition did not overstate the situation yesterday, when he pointed out the inadequacy of the particular program of double depreciation brought in by this government.
I read the speech of the Minister of Labour last night and I must say that when I criticized those who criticized us for talking about this problem I was not including the Minister of Labour. I was referring particularly to the Associate Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), that experienced parliamentarian who, within a very short time, has established himself in this house as one of its most beloved figures. I was, however, disappointed in the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) because he did not address himself to the real criticisms of this program offered by the Leader of the Opposition.
The background of this situation is simply this. On December 20 the Minister of Finance, in the only reference to unemployment in the budget speech, said that he was going to bring forward a program of accelerated depreciation to assist in the relocation of industries in depressed areas and to encourage industries to stay in those depressed areas. It was not until March 2, some two and a half months later, in spite of questions repeatedly put to the minister that we were in a position to gather what the details of this policy were going to be.
I say without fear of contradiction that any government that delays for two and a half months in outlining a program announced before Christmas in an emergency session designed to deal with unemployment is a government that deserves to be indicted for its failure to deal with unemployment courageously and effectively.
Compare that failure with the action taken in the United States. We have been asking this government for three years to study the problem of depressed areas. We have been asking the government to set up a committee in this house so we could examine into this problem. The only committee that was set up was one set up in the other place, where very important work is being carried out.

Let us face this problem seriously. We are legislators. We are dealing with an important national problem. Let us ask ourselves what industry would move, for instance, from the relatively prosperous area of Hamilton in order to settle in an acknowledged depressed or distressed area, or area of chronic unemployment, on the basis of this particular program which is to be in operation for not more than one year. Does anyone seriously think that this is a substantial program? Does the Minister of Labour not feel he has been considerably embarrassed by having to present this anaemic child born of this lethargic, inactive and tired administration?
This program of tax incentives, of accelerated depreciation, is a program which, if it were carefully conceived, could likely provide a substantial partial solution to the problem of unemployment in depressed areas. In my own area I can see where a program of real tax incentives, of real accelerated depreciation extended over a long period, could provide encouragement for the relocation of industry and for industry to stay in that area. Incidentally-and the minister did not refer to it last night-the community which I represent has made an application for the kind of limited assistance available under this program. As I say, if it were executed with sufficient boldness and scope, such a program could be of considerable use. But the program as now presented to us will not bring one industry to one community in this country. The government in offering such a program will be able to do only one thing, and that is to go out in public meetings, where there will not be full opportunity to examine the program, and say: look what we have done; we have brought in this program of tax incentives, of double depreciation, along with the scheme for productivity councils, the legislation to assist small business, and so on. Yet those men in the opposition have done nothing to help us solve this problem of unemployment. I say to the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Trade and Commerce,

the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) that it is a disgrace for the government to have brought forward a program of this kind when everyone knows it is completely insufficient and lacking in any real substance.
The first major weakness is that it attempts to foist on to the local authorities responsibility for the determination of what is a labour surplus area. Imagine imposing upon the local authorities of our country the responsibility for determining whether or not they are distressed areas. What is being done in England? What is being done in the United States by governments courageous enough to face this problem and acknowledge its seriousness? Of course, in England they have only about 1 per cent of their work force out of employment while in Canada we have almost 12 per cent of our work force out of work. President Kennedy did not hesitate to suggest the designation of distressed areas and to provide, within a few weeks of taking office, a program designed to assist the unemployed in those areas. I suggest that the real reason why this limited program is brought forward is that this government was embarrassed by not having brought forward a program in principle like this long ago, particularly when there was such discussion concerning lack of action in the United States at the time.
The second major weakness is, of course, the restrictive character of the criteria which are to be used to define a depressed area. Imagine places such as Elliot Lake, Spring-hill and Peterborough not being able to qualify for this kind of limited assistance. The requirement that one should go back to 1953 is a most ridiculous requirement. The only requirement which should have been put into this measure is: what is the level of unemployment and distress in these particular areas at the present time, not what the situation was in 1953. Is Elliot Lake a distressed area? Is there much unemployment in Peterborough? Why not apply the standards applied in Britain? Where 4 per cent of the work force is out of work for a certain definite period, then the area becomes a depressed area capable of qualifying for the benefit of accelerated depreciation. In the United States another standard has been put forward; 6 per cent of the work force out of work for a stated period qualifies the area as one which may take advantage of the proposals for tax relief or accelerated depreciation.
I suggest to the government that they are fooling no one with this program. They are not going to fool the municipalities. They are not going to fool corporations which would like to take advantage of such a

scheme. Every paper in Canada which has commented on this program has criticized it because of its restricted character. It has been criticized in the Halifax Herald, the Windsor Star, the Toronto Globe and Mail, and in papers all over the country, added to which there is the criticism I have read from the Financial Post. This is a facade which is another attempt on the part of this government to give the impression that it is doing something substantial to relieve the most serious single domestic problem facing the people of Canada today.
Something must be done about this situation. We cannot allow this government to continue in its leisurely, laissez faire way because if we do so we shall run into very serious situations. The recession may lift, but unemployment will persist and with it will come those influences which will bring about a kind of society which the Associate Minister of National Defence deplores no less than does everyone in this house.
The governor of the Bank of Canada has some views on unemployment and we ask the government to address itself to the solutions which he advances and to say whether they are right or not. Mr. Coyne, according to his report, said:
Economic developments have not been of such a character as to raise employment in step with the increase in the labour force.
Does the government agree with this statement? Does it confront the situation? Does it say the governor of the Bank of Canada is doing a disservice to this nation by pointing out what he believes to be the facts?
Then, the governor of the Bank of Canada says:
Analysis of Canada's situation seems to me to indicate that the approach to higher employment and output should be through measures designed to reduce the large deficit in our current account balance of payments and through increases in spending of a selective character likely to increase production in Canada, rather than through measures designed to raise the level of total spending by Canadians.
Does the government agree with this statement? There is a proposal by the governor of the Bank of Canada for a solution of this problem, and yet ministers sit in their seats day after day refusing to say whether they agree with the governor of the bank or not.
Then, the governor of the Bank of Canada goes on to say:
We should not allow exaggerated ideas about the influence of monetary policy to distract us from pursuing outside the monetary field the most practical and effective measures to ensure the restoration of a high level of employment and the reduction of unemployment to the minimum level.

Mr. Coyne says that the problem of unemployment belongs to the government; but, while that is the case, he nevertheless proposes his solutions for dealing with it. The governor of the Bank of Canada is a responsible, distinguished public servant in our country. I am not now commenting on whether I agree with his detailed analysis and his proposed solution. What I am pointing out is that the governor of the Bank of Canada may have exceeded his normal function, perhaps in the national interest, as he sees it, and has pointed out to the Canadian people and to the government the general lines of an attack on unemployment. He says that monetary policy is his responsibility. That is true. By that he does not mean to imply that the government has no responsibility in the final analysis, but he makes that remark so that it will be clear that with regard to debt management, fiscal and financial policy, in so far these have anything to do with the maintenance of our standard of living, they are a responsibility which belongs in the first instance to the government.
I say that if the government is serious about trying to resolve this problem of unemployment it cannot leave untouched and unnoticed these declarations of the governor of the Bank of Canada. It cannot simply hope that parliament will prorogue and that there will be no debate on the merits of the proposals put forward by the governor of the Bank of Canada.
An attempt to resolve this problem of unemployment should involve the careful consideration and study of the recommendations of the governor of the Bank of Canada. I raise this matter of the bank and unemployment at this time because I think it is basic and because, from all that one can hear, I believe the government is about to take this matter out of the hands of parliament. Mr. Speaker, I was very happy to hear the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) read the amendment presented to the house yesterday. No doubt his intention was to draw the attention of the house to the fact that he was going to speak on the subject of the amendment, limited as it is, but nevertheless he did find an opportunity to bring in a few other things which are not in the amendment. At the request of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) I should like to draw the attention of the house to a statement made by the hon. member for Essex East to the effect that there was real despair in Toronto. The statement referred to by the hon. member appeared to be a statement by Mayor Phillips of Toronto. The article in question in the Toronto Star of today is written by Dinah Kerr and in it she is addressing herself to Mayor Phillips and telling him that there is real despair. The article was misrepresented to the house by the hon. member for Essex East.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) endeavoured to bring the word McCarthyism into his speech. How far are they going to go in the making of such representations in the house with the intention, though I would not say it was deliberate, of misleading the house? While I am on the subject of McCarthyism, which was mentioned yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition, I wonder whether he is aware of the speech made in Brantford by the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) in which she said that the young Liberals should be the radicals of the party. Accompanying her on that trip was the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) who apparently aspires to the leadership of the Liberal party and possibly is trying to create dissension in the Liberal ranks. Moreover, does the Leader of the Opposition not know of the statement made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) that in the C.B.C. there are subversive elements? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, where is the McCarthy in the House of Commons?
I should now like to deal with the amendment. There is an attempt on the part of the opposition to segregate each piece of legislation which has been presented to the house. It seems that they do not realize that the legislation whereby double depreciation will be granted to those establishing plants in depressed areas is part of an over-all plan. We cannot look upon the amendment strictly from the point of view of the effects that double depreciation will have on the economy but rather we should regard the provision of double depreciation as another well advised and well planned move. To use the words of
Labour Conditions
the Leader of the Opposition when he spoke yesterday, it is another form of the massive attack upon the problems with which the government is confronted.
We are not going to be swayed by desperation as the opposition was during their last days in office nor are we going to approach the solution of these problems in other than a well moderated way in accordance with normal business procedure. The government is not going to be swayed by the woeful, sad and pitiful cries of the opposition, or by their exaggerated and often irresponsible statements. Rather, Mr. Speaker, the challenge to rectify the ills of the economy is accepted by the government and the problems will be dealt with with moderation and from the point of view of real expediency and not in a wasteful way through desperation.
The first measure introduced during the present session of parliament dealt with loans to small business. The effects are good. Then there was the creation of a productivity council. These two measures will enable the production of more and better goods and ultimately will mean more people on the payroll. Then there is the extension to $35,000 of the amount on which the minimum 21 per cent corporation tax applies, which is an additional tax concession to small industries and businesses. We also have the new incentives to industries to locate in depressed areas. Are not all these measures taken together an indication of sound planning and of the fact that the government is looking toward the solution of the problem not for a day, a month or a year but rather to the provision of steady employment and a stable economy in the future?
The government is to be congratulated for its well conceived plans and actions to bring an end to the ills that effect our economy not just for a few months but in the foreseeable future. If the former government in the days when it gloated over its large surpluses had only had the required vision it would have implemented the measures which are being introduced into the house during this session. It is not at times like the present when such measures should be taken but rather when the country has a surplus and we want to make sure that we will have a growing economy. The trouble today, and everyone knows it, lies in the fact that the gross national product has not been rising annually to a satisfactory level. The time for such actions to be taken is when governments have surpluses, because if such actions are taken then the gross national product of our country would not fall in the following years. This is one area of the economy, Mr. Speaker, in which the former

Labour Conditions
government should have taken action. However, they were satisfied that nothing would happen in the next year. The former administration should have introduced those measures which have been lately introduced, and then today we would be happy to hail them for their generous actions.
There has been some talk about tax cuts. Is this double depreciation not a form of tax cut? Is the measure raising the level at which corporations would be liable for the minimum tax of 21 per cent from $25,000 to $35,000 not a tax cut? These, Mr. Speaker, are the incentives and the means by which industry will expand and enable us to attain our ultimate goal which is full employment. I can think of many areas in the country which would be very happy if this double depreciation applied to them. I can think of plants which have been closed; and if an extra 10 per cent or 15 per cent of their depreciation fund were made available to them in the form of working capital, I am sure they would welcome it. I can think of other industries that have settled in one area, and if this legislation were applicable to them they would give new thought to expansion. I can picture them looking for a place in which primary products would be available, where transportation would be cheaper and where they could find a labour force sufficient for their needs. How serious can a person be when he says that such measures are not good? It is true, Mr. Speaker, that there are many people who believe that the well designed plan this government has introduced will bring our economy up to the standard at which it should be. In the years to come we shall be able to look back at these measures as the greatest pieces of legislation that have been introduced into our Canadian parliament.
I should like to refer briefly to the speech made by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) in which he stated that double depreciation was not adequate for the needs of the maritime provinces. Does he not recall that for some time APEC has requested that double depreciation be made applicable to the maritimes? Does he believe that this organization will hesitate to make the necessary applications under this legislation? I believe that the maritime area will derive a great deal of satisfaction from this measure.
I want to refer for a moment to the criticism levelled by the opposition at the fact that the municipalities themselves must make application. This type of criticism reminds me of the days when the Liberal party were centralizing everything in Ottawa. They do not want the municipalities, in conjunction with their boards of trade or other economic bodies, to decide whether or not they are depressed areas and in need of new industries.

The Liberal party is satisfied that these local governing bodies should stay at home and let the central government at Ottawa tell them what they should or should not have. The danger in this philosophy, Mr. Speaker, is that it tends to destroy personal initiative and the wills of local governments. We should beware of ever going back to the time when we would have a central government at Ottawa which would tell the local governments how they should operate.
The hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) did produce one statement by someone who was not favourable to the legislation that has been introduced. However, he omitted to read other statements which have been favourable. I should like to refer to one statement by John Meyer, the financial editor of the Montreal Gazette. He says:
The measures taken by the federal government to relieve unemployment fall into two general categories-the obvious, like housing funds and railway construction, and the not so obvious, like doubled depreciation and long term export credit financing. Of the two, the latter will have the greatest effect over the long run. Their common purpose is to encourage the increase in production upon which the increase in employment depends.
When we encourage secondary industries to establish in depressed areas, Mr. Speaker, we are not only increasing the employment opportunities in that area but we are making available to the other parts of Canada the benefits to be derived from the purchase of heavy equipment, building material and other products. This measure, therefore, affects not only a sector, but Canada as a whole. I believe this has been a very commendable move on the part of the government.
Reference has been made also to the programs adopted in Great Britain, the United States, France and other countries for dealing with this problem. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) no doubt had a lapse of memory when he referred to these programs because, until these remarks were made, he led us to believe that Canada had a monopoly on this problem.
Before concluding my remarks I should like to stress the fact that the opposition should take a positive approach to these problems and endeavour to bring forward some solutions. Reference has been made to a press release issued yesterday by the Liberal party in which that party set out, not the 23-point program referred to by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) last nigh, but a six-point program. All I can say about this program is that it seems to emphasize the fact that the government should extend or increase contributions or renew certain measures. The Liberals seem to be sterile

of ideas because they have not brought forward one new solution. I do not know the reason for this but it seems that the only policy the opposition has is to demand more of whatever the government brings forward. Why we went back to 1953 is more than I will ever understand, because in 1953 we had the Korean war, did we not? A period of war is the only time that free enterprise has ever been able to solve the unemployment problem. It did it then because the government stepped in and took direct action that provided employment. It was not due to private enterprise at all.

This is another shining example of this government's policy which we have seen unfolding before us for the past number of years. This is the government's idea of leadership by abdication. Mrs. Louie who arrived in Canada December 12, 1957, to visit her father, entered Canada on a non-immigrant visa.

Her son was born in Ottawa August 18, 1958, making him a Canadian citizen. Mrs. Louie sought to have herself declared a landed immigrant in order to remain here with her child. Her application was turned down by the immigration department.
Justice J. M. King of the Ontario supreme court twice ruled that "under the natural, moral, common law," Mrs. Louie should not be deported.
"Her Canadian citizen son", he said, "is entitled to the loving care of his mother, at least in his tender years."
Justice King's first favourable decision was ruled out on purely technical, procedural grounds by the Ontario appeal court and the Supreme Court of Canada.

Mr. Justice Norris upheld that when an inquiry is made and a conclusion is reached by a special inquiry officer that a person is not admissible, there is a limit placed upon the discretion of the minister. The Immigration Act lays down certain conditions under which people may be admitted or refused, and the learned judge went so far as to say, if my memory is correct, that where the act speaks clearly the minister has no discretion in such a case. For example, the minister has no power to say, of her own motion: I think there is something about this case which warrants my departing from the provisions of the Immigration Act and therefore I am going to allow this person into Canada notwithstanding the fact that the act says such a person is inadmissible. Mr. Justice Norris stated clearly that the minister has no such discretion, and therefore the first point made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is disposed of. The minister has no discretion to make orders of that kind but has to apply the terms of the Immigration Act.
fMr. Pickersgill.]

This is simply further evidence of the way in which the government is determined, in every possible manner, to keep information away from the opposition and prevent its use in debate in the house. The plain fact is that the moment this document was printed, the moment this information was available, it should have been made available to hon. members who had been asking for it for days and who had a suspicion, which appears more and more clearly to have been justified, that it was deliberately held up because of the Tory convention. It would have been a kind of fly in that ointment, though it was pretty poor ointment anyway.
I say, sir, that nobody had any warrant for rubber-stamping this document in this way. If the minister's officials did it without his consent, it just shows how little attention he pays to his department; but if, as we are entitled to assume since he is responsible for his department, it was done with his consent and approval it shows the minister's attitude to parliament. It betrays that teenage mentality with respect to which the minister is such an authority.

These days, Mr. Speaker, the opposition will do anything for sensationalism. I understand that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) rose at a quarter to six tonight and, in his usual flamboyant, dramatic style, accused the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) of somehow deceiving the house or doing some terrible thing that was aimed at the dignity of parliament. I should like to explain exactly what happened in this case. A certain procedure was initiated by the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe when he was minister of trade and commerce, and this procedure has been followed since. The dominion bureau of statistics, which comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, prints two documents. The first document is a joint release by the dominion bureau of statistics and the Department of Labour, and the second is a document produced by the dominion bureau of statistics entitled, "The Labour Force Survey".
On the day before these documents are released to the press, to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), I am advised by the dominion statistician they are delivered, as they have been in the years since the Right Hon. C. D. Howe was minister, on the regular delivery at 4.30 in the afternoon-

-of the day before the release is made. Then, I understand these documents are delivered from the dominion bureau of statistics on the eight o'clock delivery to the press gallery, to the Canadian Press, to the Leader of the Opposition and to the Prime Minister. This is the normal procedure.
Today, by mistake, a messenger brought these documents, I am advised by the assistant dominion statistician, on the 4.30 delivery and delivered them to those to whom they would be delivered normally at eight o'clock tomorrow morning. This was a mistake made by an employee of the dominion bureau of statistics. All people sometimes make mistakes. Of course, it is difficult for the members of the opposition to understand how people can make mistakes. I understand from the members of the opposition that they never do make them. People are human. This messenger made a mistake today, and he would be the first to admit it. He brought these documents by mistake and delivered them to the regular list of people to whom he would normally bring them at eight o'clock tomorrow morning.
There was no attempt to deceive parliament. There was no attempt to fool anybody. There was no attempt on the part of anybody to commit some horrible crime-
They were still withheld from parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a grievance which is different from those which have been raised so far. My grievance has to do with the application of the regulations of the Unemployment Insurance Act as it concerns individual workers. During the winter months for a number of years it has been the practice of the government through the Department of Labour to advertise the slogan "Do It Now". This practice has invited the general public to have certain jobs done during winter months when labour is available. In the majority of cases this work consists of repairs or interior alterations to homes. I realize that the government is concerned about the situation of the unemployment insurance fund and that it is taking every means possible to protect that fund. I also realize that there have been abuses in this regard and suggest that those abuses should be stopped but feel that they should not be stopped in a way detrimental to those individual workers who, when out of work, have a right to receive unemployment insurance benefits, because they have been working on jobs which qualify them for such benefits.
I have in mind certain carpenters who have been employed for week after week on jobs of this particular kind. I know of a case involving a carpenter who was employed for a period of 14 weeks practically re-building a house. He was carrying out this construction with the assistance of two other carpenters. That man was disqualified under the regulations of the Unemployment Insurance Act because there was no supervisor in attendance at the time he performed this work.
I would suggest that in my own area most winter work involves repair jobs of this type, done by individual carpenters working on their own. I suggest that the owner of the property purchases all the material-such as lumber, paint and nails-which is needed for


the job, and then hires an individual carpenter to do it. If the man is not supervised by a contractor he is denied unemployment insurance benefits.
I suggest that this government, which claims to have introduced the bill of rights in order to protect the rights of individuals in this country, is not giving to those workers the protection which they are entitled to receive. As an example of this, I must say that I know of an individual employed driving a truck for an oil company. This man required certain repairs to his house and he hired a carpenter to make these repairs over a period of six weeks. That carpenter was denied the benefits of unemployment insurance and the privilege of having unemployment insurance stamps posted in his book covering the period of six weeks because the owner of the house, working for this oil company, did not leave his job to stay alongside the carpenter to supervise him. I would suggest that this is nothing else but gross injustice and discrimination.
I will cite another example, and I might say that I have at least one hundred of them which have been brought to my attention by my constituents in the county of Gloucester. A man whose family lived in New Brunswick was working in the province of Ontario. He decided to follow the suggestion of this government regarding winter work by building a new house. When the house was nearly completed he took one week's vacation and returned to New Brunswick to inspect the work which had been done. He realized that the house needed to be painted and that a porch should be added. He accompanied his father to the unemployment insurance office to make sure that if his father did this job at the fixed rate of pay he would qualify for unemployment insurance stamps. With the assurance that he would do so, he returned to his job in Ontario. A few months later when the work was completed his father who was out of work applied for unemployment insurance benefits but was denied those benefits and the six-week period of contribution was withdrawn from his unemployment insurance book because the owner of the house had not remained to supervise the work which was done.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member is presumably speaking on a grievance. He has been building houses but he has not finished them, and I respectfully submit that he is out of order.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I have been citing typical examples of workers in this country doing jobs which

would normally qualify them for unemployment insurance benefits but who are being deprived of those benefits, and I have given the reason. I suggest that an injustice is being done by the unemployment insurance commission. I have presented this grievance and related several typical examples to support it, and for that reason I submit I am perfectly in order.
I would relate one more example of this type of injustice which involves a widow who decided last summer to build a new home. She hired three carpenters to do the work. They were employed for a period of 14 weeks but again the carpenter in charge was refused unemployment insurance benefits on the ground he had performed the work without supervision. I suggest this is a further example of injustice.
I suggest that the regulations of the Unemployment Insurance Act have been applied during the last eight or ten months, following the realization by the government that the unemployment insurance fund was being depleted, in an effort to protect this fund. Since that time hundreds and hundreds of cases similar to the one I have brought to the attention of the house have occurred in my own constituency of Gloucester.
I agree that abuses must be stopped. I admit that there have been abuses. However, the method employed to stop these abuses should not be to the detriment of those workers who are doing the type of work which would normally qualify them to receive unemployment insurance benefits. If this principle is to be maintained, it means that these workers will be affected. It means that any home owner who wishes some repairs or alternations carried out to his house must go to a contractor and pay the extra cost incurred in having the job supervised.
Is this consistent with the "Do It Now'' program which the government is sponsoring at this time? Is it consistent with that program that people who have been doing this type of work for years, who have families to support and who have been depending upon unemployment insurance benefits during a certain period of the winter months, are now to be deprived of this privilege? This applies with even greater force to those who work in the summer months at a period of time when there is more employment. They may be employed for a period of 14 weeks or more, as in the case I mentioned, and in the winter, when there is no work to be found, they go to the unemployment insurance office and are denied these benefits. They then have to obtain social assistance in order to provide for their families.
I urge the minister to take the necessary steps to amend the act or the regulations 90205-6-2034
Unemployment Insurance Benefits where necessary in order to protect these workers who are doing exactly the type of work which the government is sponsoring in the "Do It Now" program.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to endorse everything that the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robi-chaud) has said and I would enlarge further on the same matter. These hardships are being forced upon the so-called casual labourers, but I think there are also other aspects of this matter which illustrate another discrepancy in the implementation of the law as it is being applied today. I refer to the farmers of this country and the law as it is applied to them.
I know of cases last summer where farmers hired casual workers to carry out some repair work on their buildings or to have new barns built. In years past these casual labourers enjoyed the benefits of unemployment insurance. Last season, however, these workers applied for unemployment insurance and were denied these benefits. My question is this. What will happen to the farmers of the country if they are not allowed to secure the services of these casual carpenters and labourers?
It is bad enough that farmers should now be penalized by not enjoying the benefits of unemployment insurance for the hired help which they need on their farms. However, they are going to be further penalized by being unable to hire carpenters to do the work that must be done on their farms. I say that this situation is very serious indeed.
There is another interpretation of this measure which works against the farming population of the country. I refer to those people who volunteer to stay within the community in order to perform this kind of work and who will not in the future be permitted to do so. I think this will mean a serious blow to the social structure of rural communities. These people will now be forced to leave this field of activity; they will have to abandon this type of casual work, which is essential to the social structure of the community. These workers will have to hire out their services to registered contractors, and such contractors do not exist in rural communities.
I wish again to emphasize that the situation will simply play havoc in the organization of rural communities. Therefore I endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Gloucester. I also wish to mention another aspect of this matter which concerns those people who are being disqualified. Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether I am in order. I ask for your guidance in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, in connection with the grievance raised by the hon. member tor Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) I should like to make a few comments. As my constituency is very close to the constituencies of the two hon. members from eastern New Brunswick who spoke previously, I think it is only proper for me to try to give some explanation in order that there will be no misunderstanding regarding what is actually taking place.
From time to time, of course, very grave injustices are committed in the administration of the unemployment insurance fund. I receive complaints in this connection, as does every hon. member of the house, but when these complaints are investigated, quite often it is found they are not entirely justified.
A great many of the workmen involved are related by blood or marriage to the property owners in question. Invariably there is no relationship of master and servant, no contract of employment, and no fixed hourly or weekly wage, or alternatively there are no fixed working hours even on a daily rate. Supervision is not necessarily all-important. There must be a contract, expressed or implied, of servant and master or employee and employer.
The same situation is found in eastern New Brunswick as is found in many other sections of the country concerning the operation of highway trucks. In some cases the driver is the owner of the vehicle but the vehicle has been reregistered in the name of an uncle, aunt, father or mother. The driver attempts to become an employee when in fact the contractor's cheque goes to him and then in many cases is turned over to a finance company.
Mr. Speaker, those are my comments in reference to the grievance which has been raised. I would emphasize that mistakes do occur. Fortunately these mistakes are not too numerous, but we members of parliament, particularly members of the opposition, take advantage of any irregularity and in some cases are not entirely justified.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to very briefly endorse the plea made by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). In support of his plea for a change in the regulations concerning the unemployment insurance administration I think he gave some excellent illustrations. I could give similar illustrations from my experience in my own constituency, but I shall not take up the time of the house by doing so now because possibly some other members may have a word to say on this grievance. I do wish to join, however, with other members who have spoken in urging the minister


to give favourable consideration to these representations. The grievance advanced by the hon. member for Gloucester was supported by what in my opinion was excellent evidence from his own constituency, and similar evidence could, I believe, be obtained from other constituencies all across Canada.

I want to support the representations made by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) and the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Michaud). The way in which certain sections of the Unemployment Insurance Act are being interpreted seems to be much more rigid at the present time than it was formerly and as a result, as several hon. members have pointed out, hardship is being caused to tradesmen in small rural communities.
The hon. member for Gloucester illustrated his point by giving details of a number of cases and I want to tell the house that exactly the same position arises in my own province. A number of cases have been brought to my attention from the smaller communities in my own riding where circumstances have arisen identical to those described by the hon. member for Gloucester.
There also seems to be some difference in the interpretation of what constitutes a contract of service. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat pointed out that if a man who owns a truck employs his son to drive that truck, the son is not entitled to insurance stamps. If the owner of the truck wishes to hire it to another he has to put in a driver other than a member of his own family if the driver is to be able to qualify for unemployment benefit. In my area there are many small shopkeepers who have to operate trucks in connection with their businesses, to bring freight from the public wharves or to deliver purchases to homes some distance from their stores. These shopkeepers, too, are not able to employ their children for these services unless those children are to be deprived of the benefit of insurance. It seems very strange to these people that they should have to give jobs to strangers rather than to their own sons and daughters if the right to collect stamps is to be preserved.
Returning to the question of the contract of service I may perhaps speak from my own experience. As hon. members know, most of my riding is a coastal region and in order to get about it I have to use a boat. The most economical way of providing boat transportation is to own a boat. Last fall I had to make a decision to have done to my boat some fairly extensive repairs which would provide at least two months' work for two carpenters. However, I was not able

to have this work done because I was not in a position to give stamps to the men while they were so employed. I took the trouble to discuss this problem with the officials of the unemployment insurance commission in the local office at St. John's. I thought I could get around the difficulty. It was clear that I could not be on the spot to supervise the work, but I thought it might be possible to employ an agent to do that on my behalf and to put the stamps in these men's books. After some deliberation and I believe, consultation with the head office in Ottawa I was told that an arrangement of this kind could not be allowed. On that account eight months' work for some carpenter has been lost and I, for my part, have been unable to get work done which is of importance to me.
It does not seem sensible to put on a big drive to encourage people to employ men during the winter months on odd jobs, and to pay such great attention to a winter works program, and then to say: these people cannot be employed and collect stamps unless you are prepared to give up your job and watch what they are doing. It seems to me that a situation of that sort is illogical and I hope the minister will do something about it at the earliest date.

Would the hon. member permit a question? The hon. member has just made mention of men working on his boat and the difficulty experienced if workers are unable to get stamps. Is the hon. member implying that people are turning down offers of work in Newfoundland because they are not qualified for unemployment insurance on the particular job offered to them?
Say, no.
